cells.tense: You are here with the pen down and no verdict rushing past the feeling.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what serves
cells.ask: Take one agreement you hold with somebody and finish it from your side. Choose the one that has already run its course, whether or not anyone has said so out loud. Then check what your hands are still carrying.
cells.core:
When two people are out of step, you can feel it to the bottom and still say what's fair. Nobody gets punished for an emotion, and nobody's emotion tips the scale. The call lands after the feeling finishes, not over it. You also carry an eye for what has finished — a habit of evening something out that stopped evening anything a while back.

What's here is letting one of those go. Not with a speech. With a choice. An agreement you hold with someone, one that wrapped up quietly and nobody announced. The cost is the ease of gripping a thing past its time. Finish it from your side. Then check what remains in your hands, and how much of it you still want.
cells.sheetLine: You feel it all and still call it fair.

cells.tense: You are bracing to deliver a ruling you already wrote over a hurt still happening.
cells.act: lay the one step you can see, solidly
cells.ask: Let the next hurt that lands on you sit for a whole day before any ruling goes out. No measuring, no deciding — hold it as weight. One solid step. The ruling waits.
cells.core:
The rulings arrive before the feelings finish. Someone is upset, and you've weighed already whether the upset was fair. Fairness at that speed doesn't land as fair. It lands like a court the person wandered into without meaning to. You are out past the feeling, past the room, past yourself.

What holds is slower and heavier. Take the next hurt and carry it through a day without measuring it — no verdict, no proportions, just the weight of it. A builder lifts stone this way: feels its heft, doesn't yet know what wall it's for. When you finally do rule, the ruling will be shorter, and the one it concerns will be able to hear it. Lay that step.
cells.sheetLine: The ruling is arriving before the hurt has finished.

cells.tense: Where things went sideways, you stood at the bench and then walked off.
cells.act: write the facts down in order, without feeling words
cells.ask: Choose one unfair situation you've stopped calling. Lay the facts on paper — then what, then what, with no feeling words anywhere in them. Then read your own page.
cells.core:
What this looks like going well: you read a situation between people, see where the weight is off, say it plainly, and the ones inside it can breathe again. The call gets made. That has been the shape of it, and it isn't here right now.

Something between people near you has gone out of proportion, nobody weighted it, and you stepped away — not in spite, just a threshold you stopped crossing. Method does what nerve won't. Take an unfair situation and lay the facts on paper, sequence only, no feeling words. Then read your own page. Putting the sequence down doesn't ask for nerve. The call is half made once it's written.
cells.sheetLine: You can see what's unfair and you've stopped calling it.

cells.tense: You keep the peace between people and tell them you had no part in it.
cells.act: perceive it with fresh eyes before judging
cells.ask: Hear the next dispute close by the way somebody new to it would, perceiving what's actually there before you reach in to even the score. Let the judging come later; for now just take it in.
cells.core:
The people near you stay level because you quietly keep them level — a word dropped here, a weight shifted there. Ask, and you'd say you stay out of it. The balance has someone minding it. That someone's own version of events is the bystander's, and the ones being kept level have not bought it for a while.

Hear first. That's the beginner's form of the judge. A dispute starts close by, and before you reach in to smooth it, take it in the way somebody learning it would — no ruling loaded, no score to even. You'll catch the part you usually smooth past before anyone says it. The quiet work of keeping things level gets seen from the inside, by the one doing it. Nothing else shifts.
cells.sheetLine: The balance between people is kept, by you, while you say you stay out of it.

The ask survives being wrong: releasing a standing arrangement teaches something either way, even if the read of the person is off. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is the one about the arrangement 'already knows it isn't' — cut it or fix it so the person isn't told what others think. Second pass: every core must name the mechanism in a moment they could recognise, and the Too Much/Too Little pair must be opposite failures of the same thing — too fast with the verdict vs stepped back from the bench.

Cut to what the person does. In the Too Much cell I'd written the hurt 'as weight' four beats in a row, which is the house's own exemplar phrasing carried too close; the ask now says carry it without ruling, in the person's own image. The sentence that serves the writer was 'the call arrives half made, in your own handwriting' — it is lovely and it flatters me, so I keep the plain version: the sequence is on the page, that's the whole of it. The four asks open on take, let, choose, hear. Closing moves differ: a look at the hands, the ruling waits, read your own page, nothing else shifts.
